Conflict Management in Intent-Based Networking

Technical White Paper

TMF C930 — Phase II

TM Forum Digital Transformation World 2026

Executive Summary

Autonomous Networks at Level 4 promise networks that optimise, heal, and scale themselves — yet a fundamental barrier remains: when multiple autonomous agents operate on shared infrastructure, each optimising its own KPI in isolation, conflicts between them are inevitable. One agent adjusts handover thresholds to save energy while another tunes uplink power for throughput; individually both are correct, but together they breach a critical service commitment that neither is aware of. Today, operators limit themselves to few concurrent autonomous processes precisely because no framework exists to detect, prevent, or resolve these inter-agent conflicts safely. This constraint blocks the transition from Level 3 (conditional autonomy with human oversight) to Level 4 (high autonomy with closed-loop self-governance).

TMF Catalyst C930 addresses this gap directly with a six-capability conflict management framework: scope governance ensuring every autonomous domain declares its operational boundaries upfront; conflict prevention translating business-level intents into enforceable network parameters with feasibility checks; cross-domain awareness sharing active intents across service and optimisation layers; pre-execution evaluation assessing every proposed action against all live commitments before it reaches the network; Gen-AI self-learning enabling rejected agents to autonomously refine and resubmit conflict-free proposals; and vendor-neutral arbitration allowing third-party agents to participate without bilateral integration agreements.

Partners & Champions

Four technology partners (Ericsson, Aira Technologies, Red Hat, AWS) contribute live components, and nine operator champions across six continents (T-Mobile, Rogers, Telstra, LG U+, STC, e&, Vodafone, Telenor, Axiata) co-create and validate the approach. Conflict management is demonstrated as an industry capability, not a proprietary feature — the defining prerequisite for safe, scalable, multi-vendor autonomous operations.

Solution Overview

Figure 1 — High-level architecture: Service Domain (left) and Optimisation Domain (right).

Six capabilities: 1. Scope Governance (AD Descriptor Triple); 2. Conflict Prevention (Knowledge Plane feasibility + alternatives); 3. Cross-Domain Awareness (one-way intent sharing); 4. Pre-Execution Evaluation (neighbour-cell side-effect analysis); 5. Gen-AI Self-Learning (Aira Naavik autonomous refinement); 6. Vendor-Neutral Arbitration (Coordination Agent standard API).

UC0 — Scope Registration

Governance foundation. Before any conflict can be detected, the system must know who is allowed to do what, and where. UC0 introduces the AD Descriptor Triple — every autonomous domain declares its Functional role (service vs network management), Topology scope (geographic boundary), and Concern (which KPIs and actions it controls). Each action maps to exactly one concern — no overlap allowed.

The registration flow: Network Operator Admin assigns topology scope (Stockholm) to both SO/SA IMF and IMF rApp. Each fetches its scope and registers its actions with the Coordination Agent — slice configurations for the service domain, network optimisation parameters (A5 threshold, UL P0, SSB boosting, UL BLER target) for the optimisation domain. Third-party rApps (Agent D) onboard via the same single mechanism. Overlap detection is switched on — the invisible foundation for all subsequent conflict analysis.

Figure 3 — UC0 registration flow. Three agents register via the Coordination Agent — no bilateral integration required.

UC1 — Conflict Prevention (B2B Slice Provisioning)

Figure 4 — UC1 service qualification: customer requirements translated through TMF645/641, assessed by the Knowledge Plane, validated against O-Cloud Manager availability.

Alternatives instead of rejections. A RoboFleet customer requests a persistent autonomous robotics slice — 100 delivery robots with dual-camera video, real-time voice via cloud LLM, and ultra-reliable navigation — across Stockholm. A Priority-1 First Responders slice is already active on coverage cells A, C with strict SLA: 50 Mbps UL, 100 Mbps DL, 10 ms latency. The SO/SA IMF's Proposal Agent translates business intent into network parameters via the Knowledge Plane. The Evaluation Agent queries Orchestration and detects a resource shortfall: per-cell UL demand (~125 Mbps) exceeds available headroom (~80 Mbps) after P1 protection.

Rather than a flat rejection, the Knowledge Plane generates exactly three alternatives — each relaxing a single axis while fully protecting the P1 SLA. Alternative 1 relaxes quality (2K video, 75/150 Mbps, 100% guarantee). Alternative 2 relaxes device count (4K video, 20 devices, 100% guarantee). Alternative 3 relaxes guarantee (4K video, 40 devices, 80% guarantee). The customer selects Alternative 1: adaptive video for all 100 robots at full guarantee. BSS places a TMF641 Service Order; slice provisioned on cells B, D, E via Orchestration. Revenue retained; P1 never degraded; qualification turnaround drops from days to seconds.

The Knowledge Plane uses four governed sources: Ontology (interprets business terms like autonomous_robotics_fleet), Topology (resolves address → coverage zone → gNB → target cells), Service Profiles (maps workloads to parameters with degradation ladders), and Negotiation Policy (defines customer tolerance bounds and utility weights). Core invariants: P1 absolutely protected, exactly three alternatives, single-axis relaxation per alternative, recommended alternative preserves full device count at 100% guarantee — quality sacrificed first.

UC2 — Intent Sharing

Figure 5 — UC2: SMO Service Management pushes a Resource Intent to the IMF rApp. rApp-based Agents interact bidirectionally for proposals and evaluation.

Intents as guardrails. After UC1 provisioning completes, the SO/SA IMF shares both active service intents with the IMF rApp: P1 First Responders on coverage cells A, C (50 Mbps UL, 100 Mbps DL, 10 ms latency, never degrade) and P2 RoboFleet on capacity cells B, D, E (75 Mbps UL, 150 Mbps DL, 20 ms latency). These shared intents become the guardrails against which every future rApp proposal is evaluated — no action that violates an active commitment can reach the network.

The SO/SA IMF retains full authority over provisioning and assurance. The IMF rApp uses the shared intents as enforceable constraints: before any rApp action is approved, it is assessed against this live intent set, including indirect impacts via the neighbour-cell graph. The intent set updates automatically as services are provisioned or retired — the guardrails stay current without manual intervention.

Without intent sharing, rApps tune network parameters (handover thresholds, power levels, signal boosting) without any awareness of what business commitments are live on the same infrastructure. Conflicts are detected only hours later through KPI regressions or customer complaints. With intent sharing, the optimisation domain has continuous awareness of what it must protect. Mean-time-to-detect drops from hours to zero: prevention replaces detection.

UC3 — Conflict Resolution & Self-Learning

Figure 6 — Agent C self-learning cycle: rejection → Gen-AI analysis → scope narrowing → v2 package → hot-swap → resubmission → approval.

Gen-AI rApp refinement — the Level 4 differentiator. Network Operations Engineers issue an operational intent: reduce energy consumption on capacity cells, Stockholm, off-peak. Three rApps independently propose optimisation actions. The IMF rApp performs a what-if assessment for each, walking the neighbour-cell graph to predict both direct and indirect SLA impact against the two active service intents shared in UC2.

Agent A (Ericsson) proposes reducing the A5 handover threshold on Cell B — rejected (final). Reducing A5 triggers earlier handover from Cell B to its coverage neighbour Cell A. Cell A hosts P1 First Responders. Side effect degrades P1 SLA. No sub-scope of Cell B avoids this impact because Cell A is its only coverage neighbour. Agent B (Ericsson) proposes increasing UL P0 on Cells A, C — approved. Raising UL power improves uplink SINR on coverage cells. No negative impact on any active service intent. Agent C (Aira) proposes deactivating SSB boosting on Cells D, E — rejected (refinable). Cell D's coverage bleeds into Cell C, which hosts P1. But Cell E has no side effect on any coverage cell — the scope is splittable.

Agent C forwards the structured rejection (containing the conflict geometry, affected cells, and protected intent) to Aira Naavik Gen-AI tool. Naavik analyses the report: Cell D has a side effect on Cell C (coverage bleed) → unsafe. Cell E has no side effect on coverage cells A or C → safe. Naavik generates updated business logic scoped to Cell E only, submits a v2 rApp package to the rApp Manager. The rApp Manager validates and hot-swaps Agent C → v2 (in-place upgrade). Agent C v2 resubmits: "Deactivate SSB boosting on Cell E only." IMF rApp re-evaluates: Cell E → Cell C relationship confirmed as no side effect. No conflict detected. Approved. Two actions enforced: UL P0 increase on Cells A, C (Agent B) and SSB boost off on Cell E (Agent C v2). Energy saved; both SLAs intact; no human touched code.

UC4 — Cross-Vendor Action Arbitration

Figure 7 — AD scope enforcement and coordination layer arbitrates actions across three domains. Any vendor participates through a single standard interface.

Vendor-neutral coordination. In a multi-vendor RAN ecosystem, third-party rApps cannot safely participate without bilateral integration agreements with every IMF already deployed. Each new vendor requires custom API adapters, protocol translation, and coordination logic — at approximately $150K per integration (internal model). This cost barrier limits operators to a small pool of first-party rApps, constraining innovation and preventing a competitive multi-vendor rApp marketplace.

UC4 demonstrates what happens when a third-party rApp — part of another autonomous domain — attempts to make changes on the network. The third-party rApp submits an action claim through a standard API to the Scope and Coordination Management element in the architecture. This element is able to predict the indirect conflicts that could arise from that change: if there is an adjustment that causes a side effect on a neighbouring cell, that will be detected. The system understands that the IMF rApp in the optimisation domain is the owner of that cell being side-affected, and asks permission from that owning autonomous domain. Only if the owning domain confirms there is no side effect is the action authorised — and then the Non-RT RIC will perform that action on the RAN.

The key outcome: one API, any vendor, same protection. No bilateral integration required. Per-vendor integration cost reduced by approximately 90% (internal model). This enables operators to source rApps from a competitive multi-vendor marketplace, with the Scope and Coordination Management element ensuring safe coexistence through the proposed TMF Open API for AD Scope Enforcement and Coordination.

Business Value

Conflict management enables the autonomy that delivers value — it does not claim direct savings. Three pillars: OPEX >30% (via concurrent rApp autonomy), churn reduction (P1 protection guarantees), new revenue at scale (automated service acceptance).

New Proposed API: AD Scope Enforcement & Coordination

The key standards contribution — a new TMF Open API standardising scope registration, overlap detection, action claim arbitration, and enforcement validation. Governed by five principles:

1. Protect the Network — every action evaluated before execution, no exceptions. 2. Scope with Authority — AD Descriptor Triple declarations are authoritative and enforced. 3. Authorization Enforced — no rApp executes outside registered scope. 4. Authorization Exclusive — each action on a given cell granted to one domain at a time. 5. Enforcement Layer Catches Unauthorized Actions — CM Actuations validates even if coordination is bypassed; unauthorized actions execute only with authorised domain approval.

Conclusion

TMF C930 demonstrates conflict management as the missing prerequisite for Level 4 autonomous networks. Five use cases prove the complete lifecycle — from scope registration to Gen-AI self-learning to cross-vendor arbitration. The proposed TMF Open API for AD Scope Enforcement and Coordination enables industry-wide adoption.
